passages.original: Minerve], et Alexander, non tam sanguine, quam religione concordes, no- susceptum opus dimitterem prophetarum, et ex- traordinario vobis labore sudarem, breviter in Prooemio sum locutus : ut proponens verba Mala- chi, primum juxta Hebraicam veritatem, deinde juxta LXX interpretes, orationum vestrarum fultus auxilio, edisseram quae sequuntur. Scripsit in hunc librum Origenes tria volumina; sed historiam om- nino non tetigit, et more suo totus in allegoriae interpretatione versatus est, nullam [Al. non ullam] Ezrae faciens mentionem : sed angelum putans fuis- se qui scripsit, secundum illud quod de Joanne legimus : Ecce ego mitto angelum meum ante faciam tuam2 (Matth.XI, 10).
passages.english: These things, my Minervius [another reading: Minerve], and Alexander, you who are united not so much by blood as by religion, I have stated briefly in the Preface, so that I would not abandon the work on the prophets that I had undertaken and toil for you at an extraordinary labour: so that, setting out the words of Malachi first according to the Hebrew truth and then according to the Seventy translators, and supported by the help of your prayers, I may expound what follows. Origen wrote three volumes on this book, but he did not touch the historical sense at all. As is his custom, he was wholly occupied with allegorical interpretation, making no mention [another reading: not any mention] of Ezra; instead he thought that it was an angel who wrote [it], in accordance with what we read concerning John: "Behold, I send my angel before your face" (Matt. 11:10).
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; "These things" (Haec) comes from the preceding context. "no-" at the line break has been read as "ne" ("so that I would not"). "faciam" is read as "faciem" ("face"), and the footnote numeral has been omitted. "Angelum" can mean both "angel" and "messenger". Origen's reading turns on the name Malachi ("my angel/messenger"), whereas Jerome identifies the prophet with Ezra.
